questions.q: What are the six SDLC phases?
options: Idea, code, merge, release, bill, retire
Requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance
Plan, build, test, ship, sell, support
Sprint, review, retro, plan, demo, ship
questions.explain: Every methodology arranges and repeats the same phases.

questions.q: How do Waterfall and Agile differ regarding the phases?
options: Not which phases exist, but how often you cycle through them and in what order
questions.explain: Waterfall runs them once; Agile runs a compressed version repeatedly per sprint.

questions.q: What is the typical output of the Requirements phase?
options: Requirements document, user stories, acceptance criteria
questions.explain: Design produces architecture diagrams and data models.

questions.q: What does the Maintenance phase involve?
options: Bug fixes, patches, feature updates and monitoring
questions.explain: It continues after deployment.

questions.q: What is Waterfall?
options: The SDLC run once, in strict sequence, with a formal sign-off gate between phases
questions.explain: Winston Royce described it in 1970 as a risky approach to warn against.

questions.q: Why is it costly when Testing reveals a wrong requirement?
options: Each gate is expensive to reopen: a formal change request, re-approval and rework of downstream artifacts
questions.explain: That's the defining trait of Waterfall.

questions.q: When does Waterfall genuinely fit?
options: Stable requirements, fixed-price contracts, safety-critical or heavily audited work
questions.explain: Up-front certainty is rewarded.

questions.q: Who typically signs off Testing → Deployment?
questions.explain: All defined test cases pass with no open critical defects.

questions.q: Where and when was the Agile Manifesto written?
options: February 2001, Snowbird, Utah, by seventeen practitioners
questions.explain: They were frustrated with heavyweight documentation-driven processes.

questions.q: What is the key caveat in the Manifesto?
options: Items on the right are banned
While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more
questions.explain: Agile doesn't mean no process, no documentation, no contracts or no planning.

questions.q: What does 'working software over comprehensive documentation' mean?
options: Documentation is still valued, but working software outranks it
questions.explain: It's a common misreading to say Agile means no documentation.

questions.q: How many principles back the four values?
questions.explain: For example deliver working software frequently, in weeks rather than months.

questions.q: What are Scrum's parts?
options: Three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts
questions.explain: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers.

questions.q: Is the Daily Scrum a status report to the Scrum Master?
options: No: it's Developers inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal and re-planning the next 24 hours (15 minutes)
questions.explain: Running it as a status meeting is a role failure.

questions.q: What is the real output of the Sprint Review?
options: An updated Product Backlog, from stakeholder feedback on the Increment
questions.explain: It's not a demo for its own sake.

questions.q: What is a common Product Owner failure?
options: Acting as a project manager in disguise, assigning tasks and dictating how work happens
questions.explain: That collapses self-organisation and turns Scrum into Waterfall with a two-week clock.

questions.q: Kanban is flow-based. What does that mean versus Scrum?
options: No sprints or timeboxes; work flows continuously across a visual board regulated by WIP limits
questions.explain: The original method has no dedicated Product Owner.

questions.q: Development is full (4/4). A developer finishes early. What should they do?
options: Help unblock items stuck downstream (e.g. Review), not pull a new item
questions.explain: Pull means work enters a stage only when there is capacity downstream.

questions.q: Why are WIP limits the whole point?
options: They fight the instinct to start work, since a pile of half-finished work is worse than an idle hour
questions.explain: Teams should be measured on what's finished, not started.

questions.q: One column is perpetually full. What does it reveal?
options: That stage is the bottleneck; add capacity there
questions.explain: Lots of items in progress but few finished means too much WIP.

questions.q: What is the decision test between Agile and Waterfall?
options: Which of scope, schedule or cost is truly fixed; the other two must flex
questions.explain: Fixed scope fits Waterfall; fixed schedule or cost fits Agile.

questions.q: A trade-show launch date is fixed. What flexes?
questions.explain: That fits Agile.

questions.q: When is risk discovered in each model?
options: Waterfall: late (often in Testing); Agile: early and often, every sprint
questions.explain: Agile surfaces new information each sprint.

questions.q: What contract type best fits each?
options: Waterfall: fixed-price, fixed-scope; Agile: time-and-materials or scope-flexible fixed-budget
questions.explain: A request to 'be more agile' that fixes all three variables is incoherent.

questions.q: What is the standard user story format?
options: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
questions.explain: The 'so that' clause anchors developer judgment calls.

questions.q: What are acceptance criteria?
options: Specific, testable conditions that must hold for the story to be complete
questions.explain: For example a customer with no saved address sees an empty form.

questions.q: What goes wrong without the 'so that' benefit?
options: A developer can't make good judgment calls about edge cases
questions.explain: For example whether to let users edit a prefilled address.

questions.q: What is a backlog?
options: The ordered collection of stories and work items a team might build
questions.explain: Vague or oversized stories are where most sprint failures start.

questions.q: Why are story points relative?
options: Humans are bad at absolute durations but good at comparing sizes
questions.explain: Compare to something already built.

questions.q: What does a story point encode?
questions.explain: A small high-uncertainty task can get more points than a bigger familiar one.

questions.q: Why does the Fibonacci scale widen its gaps?
options: Precision on big items is false; choosing between 14 and 15 is meaningless
questions.explain: Anything 20+ should usually be split.

questions.q: What technique estimates collaboratively?
questions.explain: Everyone reveals estimates together.

questions.q: What does Sprint Planning produce?
options: A Sprint Goal (one sentence) and a Sprint Backlog sized to capacity
questions.explain: Inputs: ordered Product Backlog, capacity and historical velocity.

questions.q: In the example, Dev B has 8 days and focus factor 0.8. What is the effective capacity?
questions.explain: 8 × 0.8 = 6.4; the team total was 29.4 person-days.

questions.q: Last three sprints delivered 21, 25 and 23 points. What is the planning guidance?
options: Plan about 23 points (average velocity), not more just because the backlog has more
questions.explain: Velocity is a sanity check against over-commitment.

questions.q: From which end of the backlog are stories pulled?
options: The top, since it's ordered by priority
questions.explain: Running totals stop when the planned points are reached.

questions.q: Why does the capstone use a 1-week sprint?
options: To keep it finishable in one sitting while exercising every step
questions.explain: The common length is two weeks.

questions.q: What must exist before any sprint?
options: A Product Goal and an ordered Product Backlog
questions.explain: Their goal: track spending against a monthly budget without a spreadsheet.

questions.q: The team's first sprint has no velocity. What do they plan against?
questions.explain: Velocity builds after sprints run.

questions.q: How are stories estimated?
options: Planning Poker on the Fibonacci scale, with discussion to a final value
questions.explain: Differences between estimators are discussed.

questions.q: Which event checks whether you built the right thing?
questions.explain: The Daily Scrum checks you're on track for the plan.

questions.q: What risk arises from running tight standups but skipping a genuine Review?
options: Being efficient at building the wrong thing
questions.explain: Review feeds the backlog with stakeholder feedback.

questions.q: What is the highest-leverage Daily Scrum fix?
options: Reframe from 'what did I do' to 'what's in the way of the Sprint Goal'
questions.explain: Only the team can act on blockers, so it becomes self-organising.

questions.q: What is a healthy retrospective outcome?
questions.explain: Venting without follow-through is the failure mode.

questions.q: What are the five retrospective stages?
options: Set the stage, gather data, generate insights, decide what to do, close
questions.explain: Skipping straight to deciding produces actions aimed at symptoms.

questions.q: What is the Prime Directive?
options: Everyone did the best job they could, given what they knew, their skills, resources and the situation (Norm Kerth)
questions.explain: It reframes retros from blame to system improvement.

questions.q: Which techniques generate insights?
options: 5 Whys, fishbone diagram and affinity mapping
questions.explain: Dot-voting and effort/impact grids help decide.

questions.q: How many actions should a retro leave?
options: 1–3 concrete actions with owners and a due sprint
questions.explain: Fewer actions get done.

questions.q: What is refinement?
options: The ongoing habit of taking items from idea to ready-to-pull, ideally no more than 10% of team capacity
questions.explain: It was formerly called grooming.

questions.q: What does INVEST stand for?
options: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Iterative, Native, Visual, Easy, Short, Timed
Important, New, Visible, Early, Simple, Tested
Ideal, Neat, Valid, Exact, Safe, True
questions.explain: Used as a readiness gate for stories.

questions.q: Which are story-splitting axes?
options: Workflow steps, business rules, data boundaries, CRUD operations, happy path versus edge cases
questions.explain: For example Checkout into browse cart, coupon, pay, confirm.

questions.q: Who orders the backlog?
questions.explain: Estimating involves the whole team.

questions.q: What is the difference between lead time and cycle time?
options: Lead time: request created to delivered; cycle time: work started to delivered
Lead is hours; cycle is days
questions.explain: Lead time is the customer's wait.

questions.q: What does Little's Law say?
options: Average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput, so lowering WIP lowers cycle time
questions.explain: That's the maths behind WIP limits.

questions.q: A CFD's 'In Progress' band widens steadily. What does it mean?
options: Growing WIP: a bottleneck forming, work starting faster than finishing
questions.explain: Parallel bands mean stable flow.

questions.q: Why use percentiles instead of the average cycle time?
options: Cycle time has a long right tail; 85th percentile is a reasonable forecast and 95th suits external commitments
questions.explain: The average hides outliers.

questions.q: What do DoR and DoD gate?
options: DoR gates entry into a sprint; DoD gates the exit (when something is finished)
questions.explain: DoR is per story; DoD is usually team-wide.

questions.q: What happens with a strong DoD but no DoR?
options: The team pulls in vague stories and discovers mid-sprint what 'done' means for each
questions.explain: The reverse gives inconsistent quality.

questions.q: Why is DoD layered?
options: Some criteria apply to every story (review, tests), others once per sprint or release (regression suite); mixing makes it too heavy
questions.explain: Keep per-story checks light.

questions.q: In the volatile-velocity example, what was wrong?
options: The DoD only said 'code merged', so stories shipped without tests, inflating velocity while accumulating defects
questions.explain: Strengthening the DoD stabilises velocity.

questions.q: What is velocity for?
options: Forecasting how much a specific team can complete in a future sprint, from its own recent history
questions.explain: Story points completed per sprint, averaged over recent sprints.

questions.q: Why is cross-team velocity comparison meaningless?
options: Story points are relative and team-specific, so they're different units; comparisons push teams to inflate estimates
questions.explain: That causes velocity inflation.

questions.q: Backlog 140 points, average velocity 19.8. About how many sprints?
questions.explain: Present a range, not a single number.

questions.q: What counts toward velocity?
options: Only points for stories fully meeting the Definition of Done
questions.explain: Partial-credit counting inflates velocity.

questions.q: Date-driven versus scope-driven release plans?
options: Date-driven fixes the date and varies scope; scope-driven fixes the feature set (MVP) and varies the date
questions.explain: Most real releases are a hybrid.

questions.q: What if the forecast doesn't clear the fixed date?
options: Cut scope, never compress the Definition of Done
questions.explain: Quality is not the lever.

questions.q: How often should a release plan be re-forecast?
options: Every sprint, with updated velocity and remaining backlog
questions.explain: It's a living forecast, not a one-time Gantt chart.

questions.q: 95 must-have points, velocity 19 (range 15–24), 5 sprints available. What's the verdict?
options: Tight, not safe: the average fits but the worst case reads closer to 7 sprints
questions.explain: Raise it in release planning and consider cutting scope.

questions.q: Who should write a working agreement?
options: The team itself, as a short team-owned document
questions.explain: A rule imposed is compliance; a rule the team wrote is a commitment.

questions.q: Where should norms be drafted?
options: In a retrospective, where they emerge from fresh friction
questions.explain: Keep it short (5–10 items) and visible.

questions.q: How should violations be treated?
options: As a retro topic, since the norm itself may be wrong
questions.explain: Handle peer-to-peer.

questions.q: When should agreements be reviewed?
options: Every few sprints and when a new member joins
questions.explain: A new hire should read it on day one.

questions.q: What does Scrum protect when change arrives mid-sprint?
options: The Sprint Goal, not the exact ticket list
questions.explain: The question is whether accepting it still lets us meet the goal.

questions.q: A critical production bug (outage) lands mid-sprint. Response?
options: Accept it and renegotiate scope to protect the goal
questions.explain: It threatens the goal if unfixed.

questions.q: A 'nice to have while you're in there' request?
options: Defer to the backlog and refine for the next sprint
questions.explain: No bearing on the Sprint Goal.

questions.q: Is the right question 'can the team fit it'?
options: No: ask whether accepting it still lets the team meet the Sprint Goal
questions.explain: That's the decision framework.

questions.q: Last three sprints: 21, 17, 23 points. What are the average and range?
Two items failed 'Testable'. What happened?
options: They were sent back to the PO for acceptance criteria before entering the plan
questions.explain: The DoR gate protects the plan.

questions.q: Must-have is 26 points, forecasting about 1.3 sprints. Why a 10-week window?
options: The release also needs DoD hardening, deployment and buffer, which story points don't cover
questions.explain: A hardening allowance is added instead of inflating estimates.

questions.q: What do sprints 4 and 5 hold?
options: Hardening (regression, security, load) with no new stories, and a reserved buffer/bug-fix sprint
questions.explain: Buffer is held in reserve, not pre-committed.

questions.q: Why do scaling frameworks exist?
options: One Scrum team tops out around 5–9 people; many teams need coordinated backlogs, dependencies and releases
questions.explain: One PO can't hold context for 10 teams.

questions.q: How do SAFe, LeSS and Nexus compare?
options: SAFe: prescriptive, highest overhead; LeSS: minimal, more Scrum not Scrum-plus; Nexus: lightweight with an integration team
questions.explain: Nexus is Scrum.org's extension.

questions.q: What trade-off underlies every scaling framework?
questions.explain: LeSS demands more discipline and technical maturity.

questions.q: What problem arises that single-team Scrum doesn't have?
options: Cross-team dependencies, where Team A is blocked on Team B
questions.explain: Also architectural coherence and shared cadence.

questions.q: What's the scarcest resource on a distributed team?
options: Synchronous time: reserve it for what truly needs real-time discussion
questions.explain: Push status and FYI updates to async.

questions.q: Name the three time-zone strategies.
questions.explain: Each has trade-offs, e.g. follow-the-sun needs excellent handoff documentation.

questions.q: How can a Daily Scrum be async-friendly?
options: Post 'what's blocking the Sprint Goal' in a channel; hold a short rotating live window only for items needing discussion; Scrum Master follows up
questions.explain: It avoids forcing someone to attend at 6am or 10pm.

questions.q: What does a remote retro need?
options: Deliberate mechanisms like anonymous input, since hallway trust is missing
questions.explain: Psychological safety must be built deliberately.

questions.q: What is the Water-Scrum-Fall pattern?
options: Waterfall at the edges (requirements/contracting, release/compliance) with Agile sprints in the middle
questions.explain: The middle holds the most uncertainty and feedback value.

questions.q: Why do pure models rarely survive?
options: Fixed hardware lead times, regulatory gates and fixed-price contracts force some sequencing
questions.explain: Design hybrids deliberately, not by accident.

questions.q: Why is requirements and contracting Waterfall-like?
options: Client and legal need a defined scope and price before committing
questions.explain: Build and design stay Agile.

questions.q: A regulatory approval gate is...
options: A hard sequential milestone that sits around the Agile core
questions.explain: Release and compliance sign-off are inherently sequential.

questions.q: Which column makes a risk register useful day to day?
options: Trigger/signal: a specific observable that means the risk is happening
questions.explain: It converts 'watch out for X' into a checkable condition.

questions.q: Who should own a risk?
questions.explain: Fields: description, likelihood, impact, trigger, mitigation, owner.

questions.q: Where do requirements risk and operational risk concentrate?
options: Requirements early (discovery); operational late (release and post-release)
questions.explain: Compliance risk can appear at any phase.

questions.q: What do short sprints not do automatically?
options: Surface risks nobody has thought about; risk work still needs to be deliberate
questions.explain: Tag risky backlog items during refinement and resequence them earlier.

questions.q: What are the two feedback loops?
options: Planning/product loop (Scrum, weeks) and technical delivery loop (CI/CD, minutes)
questions.explain: Perfect sprints can still ship only quarterly without CI/CD.

questions.q: How is CI/CD related to the Definition of Done?
options: It automates it: review gates, automated tests, scans, CI-green merges and deployable builds
questions.explain: It removes the manual toil that makes 'done' mean 'pending a manual release'.

questions.q: What do feature flags enable?
options: Shipping code dark and turning it on independently of deploy, decoupling deploy from release
questions.explain: Trunk-based development and canary/blue-green deploys also keep releases low-risk.

questions.q: Why isn't a pipeline alone DevOps?
options: Separate Dev and Ops teams with ticket-based handoffs recreate the old silo; culture matters
questions.explain: DevOps is culture, not just tooling.

questions.q: A stakeholder asks 'Are we on track?'. What should you lead with?
options: A forecast range against the release plan, not raw velocity
questions.explain: Raw velocity invites comparison and blame.

questions.q: Which row of the stakeholder report is most often omitted but most valuable?
options: The Ask: a decision, budget or feedback needed
questions.explain: A report that never asks trains stakeholders to skim.

questions.q: For 'Is quality okay?' which metrics?
options: Defect trend, escaped-bug rate and DoD compliance
questions.explain: Points don't measure quality.

questions.q: Which artifacts should you show stakeholders?
options: Release forecast range and business-outcome dashboards; burndown rarely as-is; CFD only to technical stakeholders
questions.explain: Choose what answers their questions.

questions.q: What are the four dependency types?
questions.explain: Each has a typical fix.

questions.q: Why make dependencies visible at refinement/planning time?
options: A dependency discovered in the sprint it blocks has already cost the sprint
questions.explain: Use tags, shared roadmaps, or joint planning.

questions.q: What is a Scrum of Scrums?
options: A short regular sync among representatives of dependent teams, focused on dependencies, not status
questions.explain: It's not a status meeting.

questions.q: How can a technical dependency be eased?
options: Sequence work and build a stub or mock of the other team's API
questions.explain: Resource dependencies are fixed by cross-training.

questions.q: Which contract model fits agile poorly?
options: Money for nothing, change for free
Fixed price / fixed scope, since any backlog reordering becomes a change request
questions.explain: T&M supports iterative discovery; a cap bounds the risk.

questions.q: How can a fixed-price deal be agile-friendly?
options: Fix budget, cadence and Definition of Done, but keep the backlog content and order flexible
questions.explain: The vendor then delivers the highest-value items first.

questions.q: What does 'money for nothing' let the client do?
options: End early, paying only for delivered scope plus a small fee
questions.explain: The incentive shifts from defending scope to delivering value.

questions.q: Why agree the Definition of Done before the contract starts?
options: It removes 'done' as a dispute at invoice time
questions.explain: Also have the vendor attend sprint reviews and sample QA each sprint.

questions.q: Which debt type is the most dangerous?
options: Deliberate and untracked: a conscious choice nobody else knows about
questions.explain: It's invisible to everyone after the moment it was made.

questions.q: How should you prioritise paydown?
options: By how often the interest is paid (code changed often, causing incidents, bus-factor risk), not by how ugly it is
questions.explain: Debt in code touched once a year is low priority.

questions.q: What is dedicated capacity for debt?
options: A protected fixed share of each sprint, commonly 10–20%
questions.explain: It keeps paying down without stopping feature work.

questions.q: What is the Boy Scout rule?
options: Small opportunistic cleanup bundled into stories touching the affected code
questions.explain: Combine with a tech-debt tag and interest framing for stakeholders.

questions.q: Why choose a Scrum-of-Scrums over full SAFe for three teams?
options: Three teams are below the threshold where SAFe's overhead pays off, yet informal coordination wouldn't catch dependencies
questions.explain: It's a deliberate framework choice.

questions.q: How is the shared Platform API delivered?
options: Kanban-style with a class-of-service lane for 'blocking another team'
questions.explain: It jumps Platform's own priorities.

questions.q: How does the plan handle a fixed launch date without a code freeze?
options: Feature-flag every launch item and toggle off what isn't ready
questions.explain: CI/CD ships behind flags to shared staging.

questions.q: How is the overseas client time-zone gap handled?
options: A recorded walkthrough for client review, plus a 2-hour daily overlap window for live work
questions.explain: Async by default; sync for decisions.

questions.q: What is 'agile theater'?
options: Ceremonies exist but the mindset doesn't
questions.explain: It happens when transformation ignores how people experience change.

questions.q: Which are common reasons transformations stall?
options: Mandated with no buy-in, framework-first, middle management left out, no slack for the learning curve
questions.explain: Kotter's model maps onto the rollout.

questions.q: What does Kotter's 'Generate short-term wins' mean for agile?
options: Pick 1–2 pilot teams likely to succeed and publicise results early
questions.explain: Then consolidate gains and adjust rather than copy-paste.

questions.q: What does 'Anchor in culture' involve?
options: Updating hiring, promotion and performance criteria to reward the new behaviours
questions.explain: Otherwise old incentives win.

questions.q: How do facilitating, coaching and managing differ?
options: Facilitating guides process with no content; coaching helps people find their own answer through questions; managing makes the call
questions.explain: Conflating them is the most common new-coach mistake.

questions.q: What does a coach who always directs produce?
options: Compliant teams that never build their own judgment
questions.explain: One who never directs leaves teams flailing in a real crisis.

questions.q: What does GROW stand for?
questions.explain: Will asks what they'll commit to, and by when.

questions.q: A Scrum Master quietly cuts scope mid-sprint to hide under-delivery. What should the coach do?
options: Use coaching questions to surface the issue and the team's own insight, rather than just directing
questions.explain: The pattern has run for four sprints and hides real information.

questions.q: What is the master-level governance skill?
options: Satisfying audit, compliance and security obligations without recreating stage-gated waterfall around every sprint
questions.explain: Governance obligations don't vanish with agile.

questions.q: What agile-compatible alternative replaces a security-gate phase?
options: Security-as-code checks (SAST/DAST) run in the pipeline continuously
A manual audit at the end
questions.explain: Likewise automated logged approvals instead of per-release CAB sign-off.

questions.q: What is the design principle for governance layers?
options: Push decisions down to the lowest layer that can make them safely, and automate mechanical checks
questions.explain: Layers: team, program/product, portfolio, enterprise/compliance.

questions.q: A single CAB meeting gates every team's every release. What is it?
options: An anti-pattern: a historical control point never re-examined after agile adoption
questions.explain: Fix with risk-based, automated approvals.

questions.q: What is the core question for choosing a methodology?
options: How well is the work understood?
questions.explain: Well understood, fixed deadline leans predictive; emerging requirements lean iterative.

questions.q: When does Kanban fit better than Scrum?
options: A continuous flow of similarly sized work, no discrete projects (e.g. support ticket flow)
questions.explain: Scrum on support work creates artificial sprint boundaries.

questions.q: What helps when deep technical unknowns exist?
options: A time-boxed spike or discovery phase before any plan is credible
questions.explain: Then pick the delivery approach.

questions.q: What's the symptom of applying agile to fixed regulatory filing work?
options: Ceremonies feel like theatre; iteration adds no value
questions.explain: Waterfall on exploratory work makes the big spec wrong.

questions.q: Should a CoE mandate one framework or act as an approval gate?
options: No: it should curate practices, provide pull-based coaching and run a community of practice
questions.explain: It must enable, not control.

questions.q: How should health metrics be used?
options: To direct coaching capacity, never to rank or punish teams
questions.explain: For example psychological safety and cycle time trends.

questions.q: How does CoE shape vary with size?
options: Under ~100 engineers 1–2 part-time coaches; 100–500 a small team of 3–5; 500+ federated with embedded coaches
questions.explain: A CoE growing faster than the organisation drifts toward control.

questions.q: In the worked example, what went wrong?
options: Coaches embedded permanently and became a required approval step for process change
questions.explain: That makes the CoE a control layer.

questions.q: Why is 'Are we agile yet?' the wrong question?
options: It invites checklist theatre instead of measuring business outcomes
questions.explain: Prefer outcome metrics to compliance metrics.

questions.q: Which is an outcome metric?
options: Lead time from idea to production, deployment frequency and change failure rate
questions.explain: Compliance metrics are easy to game.

questions.q: Why track a balanced set across speed, stability, people and business?
options: Optimising only speed can hide quality and sustainability costs
questions.explain: DORA-adjacent measures plus engagement and customer satisfaction.

questions.q: What does MTTR measure?
options: Mean time to restore service after a failure (stability)
questions.explain: It sits with change failure rate.

questions.q: What is the portfolio-level equivalent of sprint planning?
options: Quarterly (or PI-based) capacity allocation across investment themes
questions.explain: The backlog becomes investment themes.

questions.q: What is the WSJF score?
options: (value + time criticality + risk reduction/opportunity) ÷ job size
questions.explain: It favours high-value, low-effort work and penalises large slow bets.

questions.q: Why rank by WSJF rather than political capital?
options: It prioritises by economics, not by who pushes hardest
questions.explain: Time criticality captures value that decays when delayed.

questions.q: What must portfolio governance not control?
options: How a funded team runs its sprints or its technical implementation
questions.explain: Govern investment, not internals.

questions.q: What shifts with AI-assisted delivery?
options: Writing code is often faster than review, testing and integration, so the bottleneck moves
questions.explain: Human review effort becomes the real constraint.

questions.q: How might WIP limits change?
options: May need lowering, since faster implementation can pile unreviewed work into the pipeline
questions.explain: Otherwise the bottleneck moves unnoticed.

questions.q: What belongs in the Definition of Done for AI-assisted work?
options: AI-specific checks such as no hallucinated dependencies and no unreviewed generated code
questions.explain: Code review must check AI-specific failure modes.

questions.q: How should AI-drafted release notes be treated?
options: Needs a human accuracy pass before anything ships
questions.explain: Don't let AI replace the team's own reflection in retros either.

questions.q: What changes at each level of the ladder?
options: The unit of impact and the skill that matters most, not just scope
questions.explain: Scope increase alone is why promoted SMs struggle.

questions.q: What do Agile Coach candidates often underestimate?
options: Letting go of fixing it yourself: coaching tolerates a team's slower self-discovery
questions.explain: Directors must speak business and financial terms.

questions.q: Which skill helps either path credibly?
options: Data literacy: using outcome metrics to make a credible case
questions.explain: Anecdotes alone aren't enough.

questions.q: Which evidence best supports promotion?
options: A documented before/after with metrics, a practice that spread beyond your team, and an honest failure with lessons
questions.explain: Certifications are table stakes externally.

questions.q: What constraint shapes the capstone roadmap?
options: An 18-month plan for 400 engineers with no budget increase
questions.explain: The CoE is staffed from internal Scrum Masters.

questions.q: What rollout pattern does it use?
options: Pilot-then-scale: 2 teams in months 1–3, the whole organisation by month 12, not a big-bang mandate
questions.explain: A change coalition includes respected engineers and skeptical managers.

questions.q: How are cross-team dependencies handled?
options: A lightweight Scrum-of-Scrums, with a class-of-service lane in the platform backlog for blockers
questions.explain: From Level 3 modules 1 and 7.

questions.q: What supports the coaches?
options: A monthly community of practice open to all 400 engineers
questions.explain: The CoE is 3 pooled coaches.

questions.q: Your project's launch date is fixed by a trade show, and scope is negotiable. Which approach fits, and what flexes?
options: Agile: ship the highest-value subset; scope flexes
questions.explain: Whichever of scope, schedule or cost is truly fixed determines the fit.

questions.q: A regulator requires a fixed spec, and changes after fabrication are very costly. Which approach fits best?
questions.explain: Stable requirements, safety-critical and audit-heavy work reward up-front certainty.

questions.q: The Scrum Master runs the Daily Scrum as a round-robin status report to them. What is the failure and the fix?
options: It should be the Developers re-planning the next 24 hours; reframe to 'what's in the way of the Sprint Goal'
questions.explain: Only the team can act on blockers.

questions.q: Stakeholders never attend the Sprint Review and the backlog is never updated afterward. What is lost?
options: The outer feedback loop: the team may efficiently build the wrong thing
questions.explain: The Review's output is an updated Product Backlog from stakeholder feedback.

questions.q: Dev A: 10 days, Dev B: 8 days, Dev C: 10 days at focus factor 0.8; QA: 10 days at 0.7. What is the team's effective capacity?
questions.explain: 8 + 6.4 + 8 + 7 = 29.4 (verified by computing).

questions.q: Backlog 140 points; the last six sprints delivered 18, 22, 15, 24, 19 and 21. About how many sprints, and how should you present it?
options: About 7 (140 ÷ 19.8 ≈ 7.06), as a range (about 6 to 9) not a single date
questions.explain: Velocity varies; a range avoids the 'you said 7 sprints' trap. Verified by computing.

questions.q: Team B's velocity is 30 and Team A's is 20, and a manager wants Team A to 'match B'. What is wrong?
options: Story points are relative and team-specific, so cross-team comparison is meaningless and invites inflation
Nothing, set it as a target
questions.explain: Velocity is for forecasting a team's own capacity.

questions.q: A team has a WIP limit of 4 in Development, all 4 slots full, and one developer finishes early. What is the best move?
options: Help unblock work stuck downstream (e.g. Review) instead of pulling a new item
questions.explain: Pull systems start new work only when downstream capacity exists.

questions.q: A CFD shows 'In Progress' widening while 'Done' flattens for three weeks. What does it indicate?
options: WIP is growing and throughput is dropping: a bottleneck is forming
questions.explain: Parallel bands signal stable flow.

questions.q: Average cycle time is 10 days with 20 items in progress. What throughput does Little's Law imply?
questions.explain: Average cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput, so throughput = 20 ÷ 10 = 2.

questions.q: A story reads 'Improve search' and is 'too big to estimate'. What should refinement do?
options: Split it (e.g. by workflow step, business rule or happy path versus edge cases) into independent, testable stories
questions.explain: Large epics are the most common refinement blocker.

questions.q: Mid-sprint, someone asks to 'squeeze in' a nice-to-have unrelated to the Sprint Goal. What do you do?
options: Defer it to the backlog for refinement and the next sprint
questions.explain: The filter is whether it threatens the Sprint Goal.

questions.q: A critical production outage lands mid-sprint. What is right?
options: Accept it and renegotiate sprint scope to protect the Sprint Goal
questions.explain: Critical bugs threaten the goal if unfixed.

questions.q: Four initiatives compete: A has value 8, time criticality 3, risk reduction 5, size 2; B has 13, 8, 3, size 13; C has 5, 13, 2, size 3. Which has the highest WSJF, and what is it?
questions.explain: WSJF = (value + time criticality + risk reduction) ÷ job size. Verified by computing.

questions.q: Which contract structure supports agile best?
options: A fixed budget and cadence with a flexible backlog, plus 'money for nothing, change for free'
Fixed price with a frozen feature list
questions.explain: The vendor's incentive shifts from defending scope to delivering the highest value first.

questions.q: A hardcoded payment provider was added during a launch crunch and never logged. What kind of debt is it, and why is it dangerous?
options: Deliberate and untracked: nobody else knows it exists, so the interest silently compounds
questions.explain: Log it as a tech-debt item and prioritise by how often the interest is paid.

questions.q: A team adopts an AI coding assistant, and code is written much faster but quality drops and reviews pile up. What adjustment fits?
options: Lower WIP, add AI-specific checks to the Definition of Done and invest in review capacity
questions.explain: Review becomes the constraint, so the bottleneck has moved.

questions.q: An organisation mandates Scrum from the top with no buy-in, and managers still demand status reports. What is the likely result?
options: Agile theatre: ceremonies exist but the mindset doesn't
questions.explain: Use pilots, a coalition, and change management (Kotter).

questions.q: Which measures best show an agile transformation is working?
options: Lead time to production, deployment frequency, change failure rate/MTTR, engagement and customer satisfaction
questions.explain: Compliance metrics are easy to game; outcome metrics aren't.

questions.q: A Centre of Excellence embeds coaches permanently and becomes the approval step for process changes. What is wrong?
options: It has become a control function; a CoE should curate practices and offer pull-based coaching
questions.explain: A CoE growing faster than the organisation is a warning sign.
